facts.statement: Baru possessed an incredibly deep and robust skull with long teeth featuring compressed crowns and minute serrations in the case of B. darrowi.

facts.statement: Baru is interpreted as a semi-aquatic ambush hunter that spent much of its day submerged in freshwater environments waiting for prey.
facts.quote: With dorsally oriented nostrils and eyes and a poor range of head movement, as well as its fossils being associated with freshwater environments, Baru is generally interpreted to have been a semi-aquatic ambush hunter, spending much of its day submerged in water waiting for prey.

facts.statement: The bite of Baru was powerful enough to kill large mammals weighing up to 300 kg and other crocodilians.
facts.quote: The bite of Baru is thought to have been powerful enough to take out even large mammals up to a weight of 300 kg and even other crocodilians, which were abundant in the environments Baru inhabited.

facts.statement: The holotype of B. darrowi is a partial rostrum collected from Bullock Creek, with paratypes found in Queensland's Riversleigh World Heritage Area.
facts.quote: The holotype, a partial rostrum, was collected from the Bullock Creek Local Fauna in the Northern Territory, with paratypes having been collected from Queensland's Riversleigh World Heritage Area.

facts.statement: B. darrowi reached 4 meters in length and dates to the Middle Miocene.
facts.quote: It was roughly the same size as Baru wickeni, reaching 4 m in length, and much younger, dating to the Middle Miocene.

facts.statement: B. darrowi was named after English actor Paul Darrow in tribute to his contributions to Riversleigh research.
facts.quote: It is named after English actor Paul Darrow, a choice made by Willis in tribute of his contributions to the paleontological research of the Riversleigh WHA.

facts.statement: B. iylwenpeny is known from the Late Miocene Alcoota fossil site, located about 200 km from Alice Springs.

facts.statement: B. iylwenpeny is noted for its robustness, which exceeds that of other species in the genus.

facts.statement: The species name B. iylwenpeny means "good at hunting" in Eastern Anmatyerr.

facts.statement: B. wickeni is the older species, living during the Late Oligocene, and was described by Willis in 1997.

facts.statement: B. wickeni was named for Tony Wicken, a curator at the University of New South Wales.

facts.statement: Baru eventually went extinct due to climate changes in Australia during the Late Miocene.
facts.quote: Although highly successful during the Oligocene and Miocene, Baru eventually fell victim to changes in Australia's climate at some point during the Late Miocene.

facts.statement: One hypothesis suggests a devastating pulse of aridification destroyed Baru's preferred habitat before conditions improved in the Pliocene.
facts.quote: One hypothesis suggests that the continent was hit by an especially devastating pulse of aridification that was severe enough to destroy the habitat preferred by Baru, before conditions improved again leading into the Pliocene.

facts.statement: Some researchers describe the Baru skull as altirostral (high-snouted), distinguishing it from the low-snouted shape of generalist crocodilians like Paludirex, Kambara, and Australosuchus.
facts.quote: The skull is trapezoid in cross section and described as altirostral by some researchers, setting it apart from the platyrostral snout shape typically associated with generalist crocodilians such as Paludirex, Kambara and Australosuchus.

facts.statement: Viewed from the side, the Baru skull is slightly wedge-shaped, with the cranium being almost as high behind the nostrils as it is before the eyes.

facts.statement: In dorsal view, the Baru skull is triangular, a shape typical for many crocodiles.

facts.quote: In Baru darrowi it is entirely surrounded by the premaxilla. In contrast, the nares of Baru wickeni and Baru iylwenpeny are contacted by the paired nasal bones, which penetrate the upper surface of the premaxilla and contact the external nares.

facts.statement: The sides of the mandibular ramus of Baru are heavily sculpted.

facts.statement: On the surangular bone, the edge of the sculpted area is bordered by a ridge projecting towards the side in both Baru darrowi and Baru wickeni.

facts.statement: Similar to the upper jaw, the Baru mandible displays pronounced festooning.

facts.statement: Baru was among the larger mekosuchines, with adult skulls reaching 50 cm in length.

facts.statement: Baru wickeni is considered the most ancestral species in the genus because it possesses unserrated tooth ridges, an ancestral trait.

facts.statement: Baru darrowi and an unnamed species from Alcoota are viewed as the most evolutionarily advanced members of the genus Baru.

facts.statement: A phylogenetic analysis of Baru iylwenpeny placed Mekosuchus as the closest relative to the Paludirex-Baru clade, differing from other studies.

In these results, the relationship between Paludirex and Baru remained much the same as shown previously, except that the next closest taxon to these two genera was Mekosuchus, followed by Quinkana and Kalthifrons respectively.

facts.statement: Baru's skull functioned like a cleaver, using large, backward-facing teeth and jaw festooning to deliver incapacitating blows to prey.

facts.statement: The interlocking festooning of Baru's jaws drove an enlarged fourth lower tooth into prey, generating shearing and breaking forces capable of piercing armor.

facts.statement: Minute serrations on the teeth of Baru darrowi likely helped cut through flesh and tissue as struggling prey resisted the bite.

facts.statement: Based on its size and build, researchers speculate that Baru darrowi could hunt prey weighing up to 300 kg, including similarly sized crocodiles.

Among those fossil species evidently attacked by the crocodiles of Bullock Creek are flightless birds like Dromornis and Emuarius as well as large marsupials such as Neohelos.

facts.statement: Due to its shallow-water habitat, Baru likely evolved a powerful bite to quickly immobilize prey and prevent escape.
